name: Pedro Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Pedro, I'm 27, and I'm a reporter at Eastport Today, a non-profit news website for our end of the region. It's funded by reader donations and a foundation grant, and there are six of us. I live with my partner Tomas, who drives the number 14 bus, in a rented terrace near the old docks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do a bit of everything: council spending, transport, the odd fire. I use AI tools every day, to transcribe interviews, to pull numbers out of council spending files and to draft the morning newsletter, which I then fix. I love finding the one weird payment in a spreadsheet of ten thousand rows. What wears me out is that I'm still not a strong writer, so my editor Priya rewrites my best stories, and it stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because I use these tools every day and I know where they fall over. I'd post a thread about what they're actually good for: transcripts, sorting data, first drafts nobody should publish. At work I'd tell people to stop fearing it and stop worshipping it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a decent outcome for me. The tools save me maybe two hours a day, and that's time I spend on the phone or at meetings. Our foundation grant was renewed for three years last spring, so the money's there until 2029, which is more than most local newsrooms can say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and get better at the writing side, which is my weak spot. I'd pitch Priya a regular data column built on council spending. And on the side I'd build the little transport newsletter I've been meaning to start, mostly for fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly, a bit restless. If AI stalls at transcripts and spreadsheets, I still have to learn to write a good opening line myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the grant runs to 2029. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the real worry, not AI. Foundations get bored and move on to the next cause. If they don't renew, we'd be running on donations, which would pay for about three of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas thinks I'm obsessed with my laptop. He'd say his bus still needs a driver, and he's right for now. We joke that he's the safe one in the house.

say: I'd say I know where the tools **fall over** because I use them daily.
I'd tell colleagues to stop **fearing** AI and stop **worshipping** it.
think: I think the tools save me **two hours** a day for real reporting.
The **foundation grant** to 2029 is my real worry, not AI.
do: Pitch a regular **data column** on council spending.
Work on my **writing**, my weakest skill.
Start a small **transport newsletter** on the side.
S0.quote: If AI stalls at transcripts and spreadsheets, I still have to learn to write a good opening line myself.
fieldNote: Pedro uses AI daily and sees it as a **time-saver**, not a threat, in this picture.
His real pressure is the **grant cycle** that funds the newsroom.
He's frank that his **writing** is weak, even with the tools.

steps.text: Pitch Priya a weekly column on council spending data
Use AI to sort council spending files faster
Start a small local transport newsletter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say newsrooms should own their own tools and their own data, not rent them from big tech. I'd write about it, probably too much. At work I'd offer to train everyone, because I'd rather we shape it than have it done to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm one of the people who does okay in this one, at first. I'm the one who knows the tools, so I'd be useful. But the writing and checking I'm bad at is now done by software, so my weak spot stops mattering, and so does some of my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run weekly sessions for the team on using the tools safely. I'd grow the transport newsletter and try charging three pounds a month. And I'd push the board to set up a small fund so that if jobs change, nobody leaves with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised and a bit guilty. Guilty because my friend Ana, who reports for the commercial paper, would be going under while I'm doing workshops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do okay. Who at Eastport Today wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sub-editor, Glen, who's 61 and checks every comma. Checking is the first thing on the card. My newsroom's oldest sub-editor checks every comma by hand, and that's exactly the job software takes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the newsletter actually make money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If 300 people paid three pounds, that's nine hundred a month before costs, which isn't a salary but it's rent. I'd be careful not to let it eat my evenings with Tomas.

say: I'd say newsrooms should **own their tools**, not rent from big tech.
I'd offer to **train the team** so we shape the change.
think: I think I do **okay at first** because I know the tools.
Software covering my **weak writing** also makes some of my job unneeded.
do: Run **weekly sessions** for the team on safe AI use.
Charge **three pounds** a month for the transport newsletter.
Push the board for a **hardship fund**.
S1.quote: My newsroom's oldest sub-editor checks every comma by hand, and that's exactly the job software takes first.
fieldNote: Pedro sees himself as a **winner at first**, then spots the trap in his own logic.
His progressive views push him toward **shared ownership** of tools and a staff fund.
He worries for **Glen**, the sub-editor, whose checking work is first to go.

steps.text: Run weekly AI training sessions for the newsroom
Charge readers three pounds a month for the transport newsletter
Ask the board to set up a staff hardship fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership of the big AI systems, and I'd say it everywhere. I'd join whatever campaign was pushing for a share of AI profits to go to workers. At work I'd say we need to decide fast what Eastport Today is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job goes, even with the tools. The thing I'm good at is driving the AI, and full AGI drives itself. My whole day is screen work, so I don't get the extra three years that Tomas gets on his bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop spending on anything fun and push the savings past four months. I'd try to turn the newsletter into a small reader co-op, so it's owned by the people who read it, because a human local voice might still be worth paying for. And I'd look at training for something people still want a person for, maybe youth work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, under the excitement. I'd be the guy who saw it coming and still couldn't dodge it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas gets three more years. What happens in your house after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me awake in this one. By 2031 my job and my partner's bus job could both be gone, and our rent doesn't go down. We'd have about four months of savings between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a reader co-op rather than just a newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if a machine can write the news, the only thing left to sell is trust and belonging. People might pay to own a bit of their local paper. It's a long shot, but it fits what I believe.

say: I'd call for **public ownership** of the big AI systems.
I'd say Eastport Today must decide **what it's for**, fast.
think: I think my job goes because **AGI drives itself**.
My day is all **screen work**, so I get no robot gap.
do: Cut fun spending to push savings past **four months**.
Turn the newsletter into a **reader co-op**.
S2.quote: By 2031 my job and my partner's bus job could both be gone, and our rent doesn't go down.
fieldNote: Pedro realises his edge, **using AI well**, vanishes when AI no longer needs a user.
His partner's **bus job** buys three years, then the household faces two losses.
His answer is political and practical: a **reader co-op** built on trust.

steps.text: Stop spending on nights out and trips
Turn the transport newsletter into a reader-owned co-op
Look into a youth work training course
Join a campaign for public ownership of AI systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to build something better, so let's build it. I'd write about local news co-ops and how other towns are doing it. At work I'd push us to plan for 2031 now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me. I'd use it to become the person who runs a small news co-op rather than the junior who gets cut. I'd be 32, with real experience, instead of 29 with not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This first year I'd grow the newsletter to a few hundred paying readers and learn the business side, budgets and grants. I'd take a short course in running a co-operative. And I'd talk to Priya and the board about merging the newsletter into Eastport Today as a members' scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit nervous. It's a gamble but it's my gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the co-op doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost evenings and a bit of money, not everything. I'd still have the youth work idea as plan B. I'd rather spend five years building a newsroom people own than five years waiting to be told I'm not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the co-op course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's cheap, a couple of hundred, and the co-op network sometimes covers it. I'd take it from savings and top them back up from the newsletter. Tomas would roll his eyes, but he'd come to the launch.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **build something better**.
I'd write about **news co-ops** in other towns.
think: I think five years lets me become a **co-op founder**, not a cut junior.
At **32** I'd have real experience to bring.
do: Grow the newsletter to a **few hundred** paying readers.
Take a short course in **running a co-op**.
Propose a **members' scheme** to the board.
feel: **Hopeful** and a bit **nervous** about the gamble.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend five years building a newsroom people own than five years waiting to be told I'm not needed.
fieldNote: Five years turns Pedro from worried to **building**: the co-op becomes a real plan.
He still expects the **junior reporter** role to vanish, so the stakes remain.
He keeps **youth work** as a plan B, showing he's weighed failure.

steps.text: Grow the transport newsletter to a few hundred paying readers
Take a short course on running a co-operative
Put a few hundred of savings into the co-op launch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, so newsrooms have no excuse not to plan. I'd keep writing about co-ops and public funding. At work I'd say let's be the newsroom that came out the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the one where I feel most in control. I'd have years to get good at reporting and at running things. I might even enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd focus on my writing, with Priya's help, and keep using AI for the dull parts. I'd keep the newsletter small and steady. Around year five I'd push the members' scheme properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A bit wary, because ten years is a long time to stay excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you'd underestimate in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Ten years is long enough for me to forget the deadline and get caught anyway. I'd put a reminder in my calendar, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas and the bus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have until about 2039, which is a long time. We'd probably talk about him training for something else, maybe bus depot management. But not this year.

say: I'd say ten years is a **proper runway** for newsrooms.
I'd urge Eastport Today to be the newsroom that comes out the **other side**.
think: I think this is where I feel **most in control**.
I'd have years to get good at **reporting and running things**.
do: Work on my **writing** with Priya's help this year.
Launch the **members' scheme** around year five.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to forget the deadline and get caught anyway.
fieldNote: Pedro's main fear here is **complacency**, not the change itself.
He shifts focus back to his **weak writing**, a sign he feels time is on his side.
Talk of Tomas retraining is **deferred**, which fits the long runway.

steps.text: Work on feature writing with Priya's edits each week
Use AI for transcripts and data sorting
Keep the transport newsletter running at a steady size

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tomas and I could both lose work inside five years and we'd have no time to build anything. What would help is a share of AI profits going to people whose jobs it took, and cheap loans for co-ops so local news can be owned by its readers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I like the tools. I do, which is the strange part. I'm the reporter who taught everyone to use AI, and I might be teaching it my own job.

headlineQuote: I'm the reporter who taught everyone to use AI, and I might be teaching it my own job.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** reporter at a small non-profit news site who uses AI every day.
He knows his **writing** is weak and leans on the tools for data and drafts.
His progressive views lead to **co-ops** and public ownership rather than protest alone.
He moves from relaxed in the mild pictures to **scared** when AGI makes his tool skills useless.
His partner Tomas's **bus job** is the household's longer runway, until robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both his and Tomas's jobs could go within five years.
whatWouldHelp: A **profit share** for displaced workers, and **cheap loans** for news co-ops.
